newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia-Belarus union likely by June, official says.
newsitem.headline: Russia-Belarus union likely by June, official says.

text.p: A proposed union between Russia and Belarus could come into force by June, an official working on the agreement between the two former Soviet republics said on Monday.

"I believe there will already be a union by June," said Vladimir Grigoriyev, deputy head of a joint Russian-Belarussian council which is overseeing creation of the union. "It's the will of the people, and the will of its presidents."
Experts from both the Slav states are still working out details of how integration will take shape. Russian officials have said both countries will retain their sovereignty.
Presidents Boris Yeltsin of Russia and Alexander Lukashenko of Belarus signed a union treaty on April 2 which outlined broad intentions but was less far-reaching than an earlier draft.

A supplementary agreement on the meat of the union -- in what areas of economic, foreign and defence policies Belarus and Russia will merge their efforts -- has been delayed until May 15 to allow at least a month of public discussion.
The two presidents will receive reports on additional suggestions by May 17 and send a draft to their parliaments for reworking by May 30.

Grigoriyev said in an interview that the presidents will then sign the union agreement, which will come into effect after ratification by the two parliaments. He expects the agreement to be ratified some time in June.

Opponents and supporters of the proposed union between Russia, a nuclear power of 150 million people, and its western neighbour, which has 10 million people, expressed their contrasting views at two panel discussions on Monday.
Yegor Gaidar, Russia's former acting prime minister, said he opposed union partly because of Lukashenko's authoritarian policies.
"Belarus is a problem exactly because today they have a nationalistic, authoritative regime," Gaidar said. "Russia is above all interested in a democratic, predictable Belarus."
He cited the United States and Canada as two democratic countries with warm relations and no need for union.
"Until now not a single American politician ever got it into his head that if the two states unified it would strengthen relations between the United States and Canada," Gaidar said.

Stanislav Shushkevich, leader of Belarus until 1994, said union would subjugate his country's national identity. "Russia always tried to lord over Belarus, but it just did not know how to govern it," he said.
At another forum, Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov lobbied for union with Belarus, citing recent polls suggesting the union was widely popular.
"The ordinary people of the two republics don't see any alternative for their countries," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.
The month until May 15 was intended to give Russians a say in the issue, but there have been few public forums for anyone except politicians and the intelligentsia.
In any case, the public's opinions are unlikely to have any real impact on the integration process, Grigoriyev said.
"The process will have practically no influence at all because the draft has been set by the presidents," he said.
